Acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau (ACH) is a very rare form of localized pustular psoriasis distinguished by the presence of lesions on the distal digits of the hands and/or the feet and involvement of the nail apparatus resulting in onychodystrophy (Fig. 5) [102, 107]. It may also be associated with osteitis of the distal phalanges. ACH has been reported in patients suffering from occasional GPP flare-ups, which supports the view that those two diseases belong to the common spectrum [102].

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: H&E histology of a human periungual biopsy from a patient with clinically and histopathologically diagnosed acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau; panel a shows psoriasiform acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, a characteristic histologic feature. b: Higher-power H&E of the same human periungual biopsy in a patient with acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau; panel b shows parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses, and a mixed neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate, supporting the diagnosis.
panels.attribution_text: Zaim et al. Severe Acrodermatitis Continua of Hallopeau With Atypical Dermoscopic Features: A Diagnostic Pitfall. Cureus None. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathological features of a periungual biopsy (a) H&E ×40 demonstrating regular psoriasiform acanthosis with elongation of rete ridges (green arrows) along with dilated capillaries in the papillary dermis (black arrows). (b) H&E ×400 revealing parakeratosis (blue arrow), Munro microabscesses (yellow arrow), and a mixed lymphohistiocytic and neutrophilic inflammatory infiltrate (red star).
in_text_mentions: Based on the clinicodermoscopic findings, a periungual skin biopsy was performed to differentiate ACH from nail erosive lichen planus (NELP). Histopathology revealed laminated parakeratosis, psoriasiform acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and Munro microabscesses. The papillary dermis showed dilated capillaries, mild edema, and a mixed lymphohistiocytic and neutrophilic infiltrate. No dermoepidermal interface changes were identified (Figure 4). A final diagnosis of ACH with secondary bacterial superinfection was established.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Clinical photograph of a human patient with severe acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau: chronic paronychia, thick yellow-green hyperkeratosis and erythematous crusted plaques on the thumb, matching the captioned manifestation of the article's target disease. B: Dorsal clinical view of the same patient's hand showing yellow-green hyperkeratosis and erythematous crusted plaques extending proximally along the digits, consistent with the captioned acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau lesions. C: Palmar clinical view of the same patient's hand with multiple digits showing yellow-green hyperkeratotic crusting, nail destruction and erythematous plaques, consistent with the severe acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau described in the caption.

panels.figure_caption: Clinical presentation of severe acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau Clinical images showing bilateral paronychia with thick yellow-green hyperkeratosis and erythematous, crusted plaques extending proximally along the affected digits toward their bases. Erosive areas are visible at the periphery of the hyperkeratotic lesions.
in_text_mentions: Dermatologic examination revealed bilateral chronic paronychia with peripheral erosions involving both thumbs and the left index finger. The lesions were covered by thick yellow-green hyperkeratosis with purulent discharge upon pressure. Proximally, erythematous plaques with irregular crusted surfaces extended to the digit bases (Figure 1). Nail examination showed pachyxanthonychia of the toenails and onychogryphosis of the right index. No other cutaneous, scalp, or mucosal lesions were observed.

in_text_mentions: A complete study was performed with blood and skin cultures. No evidence of infectious diseases, such as syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), was found by blood testing. Leukocytosis and neutrophilia with elevated phase reactants were revealed. There was no specific abnormality in the results of her echocardiogram and a body CT scan. Skin biopsies were reported as diagnostic for pustular psoriasis ( Figure 2 ). Microbiological samples were negative.

panels.figure_caption: Clinical evolution of acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau treated with Upadacitinib. (a,b) Baseline periungual erythema, subungual pustules, onycholysis, and nail dystrophy. (c,d) Week 4: Reduced pustulation and periungual inflammation. (e,f) Week 12: Marked improvement with gradual nail regrowth. (g,h) Week 24: Substantial improvement in pustulation and nail morphology, with mild residual nail dystrophy.
in_text_mentions: A 54-year-old man presented with a 13-year history of recurrent periungual erythema, sterile pustules, and progressive nail dystrophy involving multiple distal digits of both hands. The disease initially developed at the distal phalanx of the left ring finger without an identifiable trigger and gradually extended bilaterally (Figures 1a,b). The modified Nail Psoriasis Severity Index (mNAPSI) score was 66, calculated across the six affected fingernails. The patient denied any history of plaque psoriasis, flexural psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, or systemic comorbidities.

Clinical improvement was observed as early as week 4, with reduction of subungual pustules and periungual inflammation, and mNAPSI score decreased to 54 at this time point (Figures 1c,d). A marked improvement in nail involvement was noted by week 12, with the mNAPSI score decreasing to 25, consistent with gradual nail regrowth (Figures 1e,f). By week 24, pustulation had largely resolved and nail morphology had substantially improved, with further reduction of the mNAPSI score to 16 (Figures 1g,h).
